html:
Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng in 259 BCE, was the king of Qin who conquered the other Warring States and in 221 BCE became the first emperor of a unified China. His title, his script and his standard weights and measures shaped Chinese government for two thousand years.

He became king of Qin as a boy in 246 BCE, with the merchant and minister Lü Buwei as regent. From 230 BCE his armies took the six rival states one by one. When Qin unified China in 221 BCE, he invented a new title, huangdi, "emperor", which Chinese rulers kept until 1912.

With his chief minister Li Si, he ruled by the ideas of Legalism: strict laws, harsh punishments and a central state. He:

  • abolished the old feudal states and divided the empire into commanderies run by appointed officials
  • standardised the script, coins, weights, measures and even the width of cart axles
  • built a national road network and joined older walls into a first Great Wall against the Xiongnu
  • sent armies south to take the lands of the Yue

He is also remembered for cruelty. Tradition says he ordered the burning of books and burying of scholars in 213 and 212 BCE, though the scale is debated. Forced labour on his projects cost many lives. He feared death and sought elixirs of immortality.

He died in 210 BCE while touring the east. He was buried in a vast tomb near Xi'an guarded by the Terracotta Army, found in 1974. His dynasty collapsed four years later.
